Reference snippets:
[SM-2722] Combustion leak (block) test. On 2010-2015 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.
[SEC 10.25] Overheating in traffic from an inoperative electric radiator fan. Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 3.4L V6 and 5.5L V8 engines with electric radiator fans. Temperature may climb at idle and in traffic, but not at speed, if the fan does not run. With the engine warm and idling, turn the AC on or command the fan on with a scan tool. The fan should start within a few moments. Repair: repair the fan circuit or replace the fan motor.
[B-22-172] Combustion leak (block) test. On 2016-2021 models, with the engine warm and idling, remove the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the test fluid. Blue fluid that turns yellow or green indicates combustion gases in the coolant. Keep the test fluid out of the coolant itself, and use fresh fluid for each test. A tester with a squeeze bulb makes the draw easier.

Our family's 2018 midsize sedan with the 3.5-liter V6 and the auto trans, just past 51k miles. The coolant level drops slowly between oil changes. I can't see any leak, there's no sweet smell inside, and it never runs hot. What's a sensible first test here?

With the 2018's V6 warmed up and idling, take off the reservoir cap and use a combustion leak tester to draw air from above the coolant through the blue test fluid, keeping the fluid out of the coolant itself [B-22-172]. If the fluid stays blue, there's no sign of combustion gases; a shift to yellow or green means they're getting into the cooling system.

Reference snippets:
[SM-7708] Compressor clutch engagement check. Applies to models with a clutch-driven compressor, model years 2016-2021. With the engine running, the AC at maximum and the blower on high, watch the compressor front plate. The plate should pull in and spin with the pulley. A plate that stays still, or cycles on and off every few moments, points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge.
[SB 70-414] Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout. Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the front seatback may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.

Shop ticket: 2017 full-size pickup, 5.5-liter V8, automatic transmission, odometer 130k. The AC blows warm all the time from every front vent, driver and passenger side alike. It was cold last summer. The blower works on all speeds. And while I'm at it, the brake pedal pulses and the steering wheel shakes when I brake from highway speed on dry pavement. It's smooth when I'm not braking. I'd rather throw a pad set at it than spend a weekend testing.

With the engine running, the AC on max and the blower on high, watch the compressor's front plate on your 2017 pickup. It should pull in and spin with the pulley, while a plate that stays still or cycles on and off every few moments points to the clutch circuit or a low refrigerant charge [SM-7708]. I won't guess at brake parts, so let's start with the warm AC.

Lights may dim only in cold snaps when a glazed belt or weak tensioner lets the alternator pulley slip. With the engine off, inspect the drive belt for glazing, cracks and missing ribs, and confirm the tensioner indicator sits within its marked range. Repair: replace the belt and tensioner.
[SEC 5.4] Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode. Applies to 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.
[TSB-5102] Flickering lights from a failed alternator diode. Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4 and 3.5L V6 engines. Headlights may flicker or dim at idle because a failed rectifier diode reduces alternator output. With the engine running at about 1,500 rpm and the headlights on, set a meter to AC volts and measure across the battery posts. Ripple should be below 0.5 V AC. Repair: replace the alternator.

Shop ticket: 2019 full-size pickup, 5.5L V8, automatic transmission, odometer 136k. The battery light comes on now and then at idle with the lights and blower on, and the headlights look dim. Revving it makes the light go out. Outside temperature doesn't matter. What's a sensible first test here?

None of the references I have covers a 5.5L V8, so I can't point you to a supported first test for the battery light and dim headlights at idle on this 2019 pickup. Do you have the charging-system section of the service information for the 5.5L V8 that you could share?

[SB 92-976] Lower ball joint play check. Applies to midsize SUVs, minivans and compact crossovers. Raise the vehicle with a jack under the lower control arm so the ball joint is loaded, and support it on a stand. Place a pry bar under the tire and lift while watching the joint between the knuckle and control arm. Specification is zero measurable vertical play. A helper can watch the joint while you lift.
[SM-1850] Brake pulsation from excessive rotor lateral runout. Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes. Pulsation felt through the front seatback may develop when rotor lateral runout is high. With the lug nuts torqued to specification, mount a dial indicator to the knuckle with the plunger about 0.5 in from the rotor's outer edge and rotate the rotor one full turn. Runout must not exceed 0.002 in. Clean the hub face first. Repair: index the rotor on the hub or refinish it.
[B-18-170] Rotor surface inspection for uneven pad transfer. Applies to vehicles with front disc brakes and a manual-clutch transaxle. Remove the front wheels and inspect both faces of each rotor in good light. Dark, blotchy patches of pad material, or blue-gray hard spots that a file skates over, indicate uneven pad transfer or hard spots that grab the pad once per revolution and are felt as pulsation when braking from speed.
[SEC 17.16] Lean codes at idle from a contaminated airflow sensor. Applies to gasoline engines with a mass airflow sensor, model years 2016-2021. Lean codes with high long-term fuel trim at idle may set when a contaminated sensor element under-reports airflow. With the engine warm and idling and all accessories off, read MAF airflow on a scan tool. Expect roughly 1 g/s per liter of displacement. Do not touch the sensor element. Repair: clean the sensor element or replace the sensor.

I'm out of patience with this thing. Pedal pulsation when slowing down from highway speed, felt mostly through the steering wheel rather than the seat. No vibration while cruising, and I'm not towing anything. I bought a used 2015 midsize sedan with the 2.5-liter four and automatic transmission; it shows 50k miles. Can you skip the testing part and give me the answer?

None of the references I have fits your 2015 sedan: the runout check covers pulsation felt through the seat, the rotor inspection is for manual-clutch cars, and the ball joint check is for SUVs and minivans. I hear you on wanting an answer, but I won't guess at a cause. Do you have a service manual section covering brake pulsation felt through the steering wheel for this model?

Reference snippets:
[B-13-064] Dead battery after parking from a circuit that stays awake. Applies to vehicles from model years 2016-2021. A module or circuit that does not go to sleep can flatten the battery after several days parked. Latch the hood switch, close the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to sleep. Measure draw with an ammeter in series at the negative terminal. It should settle below 50 mA. Repair: isolate and correct the circuit that stays awake.
[SM 3.3.7] Recharge check for repeat dead batteries. A battery that is not brought back to full charge during normal driving goes flat after several days parked even with no excess draw. After a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts. A reading of 13.5-14.7 V shows the charging system is recharging the battery. Measure at the posts, not the cable clamps.
[SM 8.3.1] Battery state-of-health test. Applies to compact sedans, minivans and compact crossovers, model years 2010-2020. Fully charge the battery and let it rest for at least one hour. Resting voltage should be 12.6 V or higher. Run a conductance or load test and compare the result with the cold cranking amps (CCA) rating on the label. A battery below about 70 percent of its rating cannot hold enough charge to survive several days parked. Clean the posts before testing.

Mine is a compact sedan from 2016, 1.8-liter engine under the hood, CVT, 183,864 miles so far. Third dead battery this month after parking it for a few days at the airport lot. Temperatures have been in the 60s. It seems to charge fine when I drive. What's a sensible first test here?
Begin here: after a 20 minute drive, with the engine at 2,000 rpm and the headlights and blower on, measure voltage at the battery posts and compare it with 13.5-14.7 V [SM 3.3.7].
Just finished that. After the drive it showed 14.2 V at the battery with the lights and blower on.
Good, that clears this area. Fully charge the battery, let it rest, and run a conductance or load test against the CCA rating on its label [SM 8.3.1].
Resting voltage was 12.7 and it passed the load test. What's worth checking now, given that?

Measure parasitic draw with an ammeter in series at the negative battery terminal, with the hood switch latched, the doors closed and up to 45 minutes allowed for the modules to sleep; the reading should settle below 50 mA [B-13-064]. Charging and battery health both checked out on your 2016 sedan, so a circuit staying awake while it sits at the airport lot is what this measurement looks for.

A pressure control solenoid that holds line pressure high causes harsh engagements and firm shifts that worsen as the fluid warms. Connect a gauge to the line pressure test port. Idling in drive with the brake applied, pressure should be 55-75 psi and rise with throttle. Repair: replace the pressure control solenoid.
[SEC 1.9] Long crank on hot restarts from fuel pressure bleed-down. Applies to 1.6L I4, 1.8L I4, 2.0L I4, 2.4L I4 and 2.5L I4 engines, model years 2016-2021. Rail pressure that bleeds down lets fuel boil in a hot rail and lengthens hot restarts. Drive until the engine is fully warm, shut it off with a gauge on the rail test port and read the pressure 20 minutes later. It should stay above 30 psi. Repair: replace the leaking injector or the pump module.
[B-24-176] Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check. On 2010-2015 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.
[B-19-157] Coolant temperature sensor plausibility check. On 2016-2021 models, with the engine fully warm, compare the engine coolant temperature (ECT) reading on a scan tool with an infrared thermometer reading taken at the thermostat housing. The two should agree within 10 deg F. A sensor that reads cold on a hot engine makes the control module add extra fuel on restart, which can flood a hot engine.

Hi. 2015 hatchback, 1.6-liter four engine, manual, roughly 27k on the odometer. Hot restarts are the problem. After a short stop at the store it cranks at normal speed but takes forever to catch. First start of the day is fine.

With the engine fully warm, read the coolant temperature (ECT) on a scan tool and compare it with an infrared thermometer reading taken right at the thermostat housing; the two should agree within 10 deg F [B-24-176]. On your 2015, a sensor reading cold on a hot engine would make the module add extra fuel on restart, which fits that long crank after a short stop.

Low pressure can produce lean codes and a rough idle; low pressure together with high fuel trims at all speeds points to fuel delivery.

This is my 2012 compact sedan. It has the 2.0L, the automatic and about 189,544 miles. The automatic slams into second, a hard 1-2 shift, and it's worse once the transmission is fully warmed up. What test makes sense right now?

Hook a pressure gauge to the transmission's line pressure test port and, with your 2.0L idling in drive and the brake held firmly, look for 55-75 psi that rises as you add throttle [B-19-179]. Run the test with the fluid fully warm, since that's when your 1-2 slam is worst and when excessive line pressure would show most clearly.

Shop ticket: 2017 compact sedan, 2.0L four-cylinder, auto trans, odometer 177,205. The battery keeps going flat over a long weekend. Once it's jumped it starts every day as long as I drive it daily. No warning lights while driving, and it isn't cold out. One more thing: the automatic slams into second, a hard 1-2 shift, and it's worse once the transmission is fully warmed up. How would you approach this first?

Start with a parasitic draw test on the 2017: latch the hood switch, close all the doors and allow up to 45 minutes for the modules to go to sleep while an ammeter sits in series at the negative battery terminal [TSB-9540]. A healthy system should settle below 50 mA, so a reading that stays higher means something is staying awake and draining the battery over your long weekends.

Dimming and a flickering battery light at idle that clear up when you rev, warm or cold, fit an alternator pulley that's slipping at low speed, so this quick visual comes before any meter work.
